text: Groups of Irish tales survive in books written on animal hide. The store known as the Book of the Dun Cow was set down in the 11th century. Old belief says it rests on the coat of a cow. The cow's gift of milk brought to mind the theme of plenty. The Book of Leinster, made in the late 12th century, joined the later Book of Úi Maine. Also named is the Book of Ballymote. The Yellow Book of Lecan was written in 1417. Each holds a mix of tales and poems, and some are even titled book, which can confuse the reader. To keep order, this work calls a full store a book and a single tale a text. The Book of Invasions counts among the oldest of the texts. It is likewise named the Taking of Ireland. The work sets out the early story of Ireland from its first days. It sets lines taken from the Bible beside figures of Irish myth. The Dindshenchas is a set of place-poems in which each piece tells the tale behind a place-name. Other Irish writing covers voyages, cattle raids, elopements, adventures, and visions. Well known among them is the Táin Bó Cuailnge. Only a fourth of the known texts exist in English. After Ireland, Wales holds a deep store of myth, the Mabinogion drawn from the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest. In the late 1800s, folklore and written learning joined forces. William Carleton, joined there by a writer named Crofton Croker, wrote out Irish legends, J. F. Campbell collected Scottish stories, and Lady Charlotte Guest supplied the first English version of the Mabinogion. In Ireland this work rose to a movement called the Celtic Revival, led by the poet William Butler Yeats.

okr.objective: The Irish manuscript books and the Cow's tale mark abundance.
key_results: The Book of the Dun cow dates to the 11th century.
The Book of Invasions tells the earliest history of Ireland.
The Dindshenchas is a set of place lessons.
Less than one quarter of the texts have English versions.
